sentences.text: The hare kept an office in the root of a beech, which Marisol found by walking into it.

She had been going along the top edge of the wood where the bracken thins out, not paying attention, thinking about something else entirely, and her boot went into a gap between two roots and stopped against something that was not earth.
It made a sound.
Wood on wood.
A small hollow knock, like knuckles on a door, which in a sense it was.
She got down on her knees and put her eye to the gap.
There was a room in there.
It was about the size of a bread oven and it had been fitted out with considerable care.
There was a desk made from a slate roof tile balanced on two flints.
There was a lamp that was not a lamp but a piece of foxfire in a nutshell, giving off that cold green light that rotten wood gives off in autumn.
And there were papers — a great many papers, rolled and stacked in the corners and held down against the draught with acorns.
The hare was at the desk, drawing.
It was an ordinary hare in every respect that Marisol could see.
Brown, long, with the black tips on the ears and the eye set high in the side of the head the way a hare's eye is, so that it can see behind itself without turning.
It was holding something in one forepaw and moving it across the paper in short strokes.
It went on drawing for some time after she put her eye to the gap.
Then it said, without looking up: "You're standing in the light." Marisol moved.
"Thank you." She waited.
It kept drawing.
She was aware that she was kneeling in wet bracken and that her knees were getting cold and that she did not want to be anywhere else.
Eventually the hare put the stylus down and turned the paper round with both paws so that she could see it through the gap.
It was a map of her wood.
She knew it immediately, and it was a good map.
There was the stream, with the two kinks in it near the bottom where it goes round the boulder.
There was the fallen oak that had come down in the storm three winters ago and had been lying across the bottom path ever since, forcing everyone into a detour through the nettles.
There was the fence, and the place where the fence gives up and just stops, halfway along, for no reason anyone has ever explained.
And there was a path.
It ran from the stile at the bottom corner, up along the flank of the hill, and over the top to the ridge.
It was drawn firmly, as a path is drawn, with a dashed line and a little scale bar beside it: eight hundred metres.
Marisol had lived at the bottom of that wood her whole life.
"There isn't a path there," she said.
"No," the hare agreed.
"I've been here twelve years.
There's no path there.
There's bracken up to here and then a bank and then more bracken." "Yes," said the hare.
"It's a matter of timing."
